title: St. Charles Theatre, the Grill Band, tuxedos and the no-smoking rule
summary: DeDroit recounts leading the St. Charles pit band, the Biloxi summer arrangement, the first Dixieland band in tuxedos, the college crowd at the Grill, discipline on the stand and playing with the Tulane band.

story.theme_name: Dance halls, lake camps and riverboat bandstands
story.community_name: Dance halls, lake resorts and where bands played

blocks.x: We were supreme for, I'll say, the other bands that made maybe perhaps a greater reputation, because they left town. But we stayed in New Orleans and made a living. And even sent the recording outfit to New Orleans to record my orchestra and other local orchestras. And the recordings were not good because they didn't demand that they sent. He was more intent on having a good time than he was making good records. But the records I made in New York in the studio, well, they were made properly. Well, naturally all the good things come to an end. I moved over. I took over the St. Charles Orchestra, St. Charles Theatre, who was playing stock. And Mr. Garinger, who was the general manager, happened to be over in Biloxi. Incidentally, I had an arrangement with Mr. Cobb and the manager of the White House in Biloxi that I would play for Cobb in the winter and play for the White House in the summer, which meant fishing and golf and good times. And Garinger happened to be over there. And he said, Johnny, you have a fine orchestra. I said, thank you, Mr. Garinger. I said, you know, that's just the orchestra you need in the pit at the St. Charles. He said, that's an idea. Come see me. I come see him. He gave me a contract for two years. And all we did was play between the acts. And that was the reason we got out of those funny uniforms you saw in the picture. We couldn't change quick enough to start at 11 o'clock at the Rosebud, because sometimes the show would run late. So we wore tuxedos. And it was the first Dictionary Band ever to wear a tuxedo. And my boys, they liked the dress. They were young. They made a fine appearance. I was the oldest in the band. And the girls naturally liked them. They knew every party. And when we moved into the Grill, which was really for the younger people and collegiates, You didn't have to spend as much money on the grill, you could order what you want. We found out that we drank R&J, which raised the price to ninety cents, you know, to get together, get a dollar. And we got to know it as the Grill Band more than any other name, the Grill Band. Everybody knew the Grill Band. And then we were smart, we played for benefits and things, and we played for bond drives. And I think I was pretty smart, but keeping the band up, up, up, up, never did let it go. I was considered pretty hard, but I wasn't. I just wanted the music to play properly, wanted the musicians to act like musicians in the middle of the day. And that's how it started. I think that's the reason why I had some success. But I always hired good men. Like one time I said to my bassist, who was one of the best in town, I won't mention his name, I said, you know I'm fortunate to have a bass man like you. Well he says, frankly, Johnny I'm playing with you because you get plenty of work. Realize there's no feeling there. So why should I show all the feeling? Play right. Look good. Act like a gentleman. That's all. That's all I ask. And come on time. No smoking on the stand. I was taught that lesson when I played at the convention at the Ishwater. The manager says, I knew it wasn't your band. He says, it didn't sound like your band and they're all smoking up there. And I said, oh this guy doesn't like smoking. So I thought about no smoking on the bandstand. And from then on that was the rule. It might have been a hardship. And if it came to a point, you'd rather have the cigarettes than the money, I'll get me another man. That's all. That's all I can tell you about. Now when I organized my band, Dixieland was the thing. Everything was Dixieland, but we did play a lot of show tunes and pretty tunes and we played some slow music because the younger people, some of them liked to dance to slow tunes. But we were getting more to people that could afford the Grinnell Hotel than the College Boys, because after I moved to Cobbs, Friday night got to be known as College Night, and we had all the young kids, but we had to take everything off the table. You couldn't leave an ashtray on the table or a tablecloth because we'd go out with the kids. But they were my success. Then we got to, it was so well known that my band used to play with the Tulane Band. They had a terrible band at that time. We would help them out, you know. Then we'd play, we'd see the game, we'd go out to the school. We didn't go many places. We went to Baton Rouge because it was a dollar round trip and something like that. But it made business. It helped. It really did help. Now, do you want to shut that off while I read this next one?
